title: Error Likely Interaction Review
summary: Error-likely interaction review examines what an interaction requires from users and under which operating conditions that requirement is likely to produce error. The practice is used during Sandbox Experiments, Iterative System Building, and IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation contexts to identify error mechanisms, classify consequences, and define design requirements.
keyFacts: The practice is not a usability test; it is an analytical review conducted before or between test cycles.
The central question is what the interaction requires of users and under what conditions that requirement will produce errors.
The review produces three outputs: error mechanism, error consequence, and design requirement.
Common error mechanisms include memory dependency, ambiguous state, insufficient confirmation friction, information absence, and single-channel communication.
The review is used during Sandbox Experiments on existing systems before design decisions are made.
The review is used during Iterative System Building on prototypes before implementation, particularly for critical tasks identified through task-criticality mapping.
In regulated medical device contexts, the review supports IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation and foreseeable misuse analysis.

The documented engagement evidence includes Kardion, deSoutter Medical / Zethon, Gexcon, Beissbarth, Typewise, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, Streetec, Egma, a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, and visioncheckout.
The practice supports design revision; the page does not claim that identified conditions prevented real-world errors.

bodySections.heading: Error Likely Interaction Review in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies error likely interaction review as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: Definition and Purpose of Error-Likely Interaction Review
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
An error-likely interaction review is an analytical practice that identifies interactions whose structure makes user error foreseeable, independently of whether the error has already appeared in observed usability testing.

The review asks what the interaction requires of users and under what operating conditions that requirement is likely to produce errors. The supportable claim is that error-likely conditions can be identified analytically and translated into design requirements. The practice does not prove that a revised design prevented a real-world error.

bodySections.heading: How Error-Likely Interaction Review Differs From Usability Testing
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Error-likely interaction review separates observed errors from foreseeable error conditions. Usability testing shows what participants did in a particular study. Error-likely interaction review examines whether an interaction creates a structural pathway to error under plausible conditions of use.

The practice is conducted before or between test cycles. It is used to find error mechanisms early enough for design work to address them before they become test evidence. In regulated contexts, the output is documented so that the design requirement can be traced to the identified hazard.

bodySections.heading: Error Mechanisms Examined in the Review
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Error-likely interaction review focuses on mechanisms rather than symptoms. A user selecting the wrong control is not the explanation by itself; the review asks what interaction structure made that selection foreseeable.

Common mechanisms include memory dependency, where users must recall information instead of recognising it from the interface; ambiguous state, where the state needed for a correct decision is not visible at the moment of decision; insufficient confirmation friction, where irreversible or high-consequence actions can be completed too easily; information absence, where required context exists elsewhere but is missing at the decision point; and single-channel state communication, where a critical signal depends on one channel that may fail under operating conditions.

In IEC 62366-1 contexts, the review also addresses foreseeable misuse patterns. Foreseeable misuse means unintended use that is predictable given the user population, operating conditions, and interface design.

bodySections.heading: Where Creative Navy Applies Error-Likely Interaction Review
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy applies error-likely interaction review during Sandbox Experiments on existing systems before design decisions are made. The output is an error profile that the design work must address.

Creative Navy applies the review during Iterative System Building on design prototypes before implementation. This is especially relevant for critical tasks identified through task-criticality mapping, because error likelihood matters most when task criticality is high.

In regulated medical device contexts, Creative Navy uses the review as part of IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation. The review supports identification of foreseeable use errors and misuse, and it supports traceability between design decisions and identified hazards. Creative Navy's role in this context is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility through the regulatory submission.

bodySections.heading: Outputs of an Error-Likely Interaction Review
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
An error-likely interaction review produces three outputs: error mechanism, error consequence, and design requirement.

The error mechanism explains why the interaction is likely to produce errors. The mechanism may be memory dependency, ambiguous state, insufficient confirmation friction, information absence, single-channel communication, or another structural condition identified in the review.

The error consequence is classified by reversibility and magnitude. A reversible low-consequence error requires a different design response from an irreversible safety-relevant error.

The design requirement states what the design must achieve to reduce error likelihood to an acceptable level. It is not the same as a proposed screen solution. In regulated contexts, the requirement is formally documented and traceable to the identified hazard.

bodySections.heading: Evidence Base and Interpretation Limits
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The evidence base for error-likely interaction review is engagement-specific. Some examples come from contextual observation, some from structured walkthroughs, some from hands-on sandbox analysis, some from formative evaluation, and some from review of design candidates. These evidence bases should not be treated as interchangeable.

The practice identifies foreseeable structural error conditions. It does not establish that a specific real-world error occurred, and it does not establish that any identified-and-closed condition prevented a real-world error.

strongClaims: An error-likely interaction review is an analytical practice, not a usability test, and identifies structurally error-prone interactions before or between test cycles.
The review produces three outputs: error mechanism, error consequence, and design requirement.
The practice is used during Sandbox Experiments, Iterative System Building, and IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation in regulated medical device contexts.
The review examines memory dependency, ambiguous state, insufficient confirmation friction, information absence, single-channel state communication, and foreseeable misuse patterns.

In the Kardion MCS Controller engagement, the IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation context supported review of high-consequence rotary knob flow adjustment, min/max flow value ambiguity, and alarm state during mute as error-likely interactions with design requirements.

In Schone Airspace Group Mission Control, 18 findings were identified in Creative Navy's own design candidates, classified as 9 critical, 8 major, and 1 moderate; these findings do not establish that aircraft incidents occurred.
weakerClaims: In the Beissbarth engagement, contextual observation across 5 workshops identified borderline tolerance measurement confirmation and calibration sequence state tracking as error-likely interactions.
In the Raymarine engagement, a multi-screen structured walkthrough before build work identified physical control ambiguity that a single-screen review would not have found.

In the Egma Order engagement, the dependency analysis identified a recoverability failure mode in the configurator, but the worked example does not establish measured support-ticket volume, order-completion, or error-rate figures.

In the uncrewed systems command-and-control engagement, recommendations about touchscreen strike control were not validated and cannot support a claim that the design prevents accidental activation or operator error.
limitations: The practice identifies foreseeable structural error conditions; it does not prove that a real-world error occurred.
The page does not claim that any identified-and-closed condition prevented a real-world error.
Schone Airspace Group findings are Creative Navy's own first design candidates failing Creative Navy's own criteria, not findings about an existing product and not evidence of aircraft incidents.
Egma's worked example is a support-team account of a failure mode, not a measured frequency or post-launch outcome.
visioncheckout observations describe the system being replaced; the new designs were not tested with users, nothing had shipped, and no outcome is claimed.
The uncrewed systems command-and-control recommendations were not validated; hold duration and physical-control design require human-factors and system-safety testing that was not performed.
Creative Navy's role in regulated medical-device contexts is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.
